newsitem.title: MEXICO: Mexican economists welcome revised GDP forecasts.
newsitem.headline: Mexican economists welcome revised GDP forecasts.

text.p: Mexican economists on Thursday welcomed a downward revision in the Finance Ministry's estimate for first quarter Gross Domestic Product (GDP) growth, saying the figures painted a more accurate picture of Mexico's economic performance.

At a news conference presenting the state of the economy after the first three months of 1997, Finance Minister Guillermo Ortiz said first quarter GDP was likely to emerge at between 4.5 and 5.0 percent -- a decline from his previous estimate in April of between 5.0 and 6.0 percent.
The final Q1 figure is due to be published on Monday.

"That is an important admission from the Finance Ministry...I am particularly pleased to see the Finance Ministry reducing GDP figures somewhat," said Gray Newman, chief economist at HSBC James Capel in Mexico City.

"The important thing is that in 1996 we had exceptionally strong growth...and an awful lot of people looked at those figures and did some misleading extrapolations, saying we can look at the future and consider Mexico to be one of those robust economies," he added.
Sergio Martin, chief economist for Mexico at ING Barings here, had also been forecasting slower Q1 growth and was relieved to see the lower estimates.
"For me it's not catastrophic or dramatic, but economic growth will not be as high as some people may have thought," he said.
He said the market consensus was now for a Q1 figure of around 5.0 percent, though his own expectation was for a number closer to 4.0 percent.
Newman, however, stressed that the likely first quarter GDP figures did not mean that Mexico's economy was weak.
"What we're seeing is a 'statistical slowdown'," he said. "It doesn't mean the economy is not strong, it's just comparing 1997 to an abnormal period of growth in 1996."
Analysts said the weaker-than-originally expected first quarter growth may be tied to anaemic consumption performance.

"Together with what Ortiz said and what he predicted, he may be hinting at a bit of surprise in consumption," Gene Frieda, economist with IDEA said, in reference to lagging growth in domestic spending.

GDP growth figures of 7.6 percent in the fourth quarter of 1996, 7.0 percent in the third, and 6.4 percent in the second were all measured against a extremely low base in 1995 -- the height of Mexico's catastrophic peso crisis -- setting up unrealistic expectations for 1997.
"The 1997 figures more accurately represent sustainable growth in Mexico," Newman added.

Economists explain the slower growth as a result of government prudence in fiscal policy and responsible behaviour from the Central Bank, which has resisted the temptation to boost money supply artificially.

But so far Mexico's export-led recovery, based overwhelmingly on its "maquiladora" factories on the U.S. border that assemble products from imported parts, has failed to benefit the country's industrial sector at large.
Wednesday's poorer than hoped first quarter industrial production numbers were also consistent with a scenario of slower growth, Newman said.

While the finance ministry said the weaker performance -- up 4.2 percent in March against 7.0 to 8.0 percent in the two previous months -- was due in part to the Easter holy week holidays, the markets were still rattled by the numbers.
In annual terms ING Barings is looking for 4.0 percent GDP growth while HSBC James Capel is predicting 3.5 to 4.0 percent. The official forecast is around 4.5 percent.
((--Mexico City newsroom +525 728 7905))
